deep.reconstruction:
Heading: 'Geburtsjahre der Göttinger Professoren 1837 Dec.' (birth years of the Göttingen professors, December 1837). This is the month the 'Göttinger Sieben' were dismissed. All seven appear on this page or the next: Dahlmann, Jacob Grimm, Wilhelm Grimm, Albrecht, Ewald, Weber and Gervinus.

Structure of each entry: name, birth year (written only when it changes), birth month and day, then a second number. That number is evidently the professor's age on taking up his Göttingen post. Checks: Gauss 1777, 30 (came 1807). Blumenbach 1752, 24 (1776). Herbart 1776, 57 (1833). Jac. Grimm 1785, 45 (1830). Dahlmann 1785, 44 (1829). K. O. Müller 1797, 22 (1819). On the next page, Weber 1804, 27 (1831) and Wöhler 1800, 36 (1836).

In later inks Gauss added death dates (†) and, beside each, a five-digit number. My reconstruction: that number is the lifespan in days, N = (date of death) − (date of birth) in the Gregorian calendar, excluding one endpoint. The computation is purely calendrical. For each person:
- Count whole years from the birth date to the last anniversary before death, at 365 days per year.
- Add the leap days in that span; 1800 is not a leap year.
- Add the remaining days to the death date.

Example (my computation), Mitscherlich, 1760-09-20 to 1854-01-06:
- 93 years × 365 = 33945.
- Leap days 1764–1852 = 23 − 1 (for 1800) = 22.
- Remaining days: Sept 10 + Oct 31 + Nov 30 + Dec 31 + Jan 6 = 108.
- Total 34075, exactly as written.

I verified all entries this way:
- Blumenbach 1752-05-11 to 1840-01-22: 32031. The last digit is blotted in the image; 32031 is the correct value.
- Mitscherlich: 34075.
- Pott 1760-10-10 to 1838-10-18: 28496.
- Heeren 1760-10-25 to 1842-03-06: 29716.
- Benecke 1762-06-10 to 1844-08-21: 30022.
- Hugo 1764-11-23 to 1844-09-15: 29150.
- Bauer 1772-08-16 to 1843-06-01: 25855 by my computation; the manuscript has 25853.
- Herbart 1776-05-04 to 1841-08-14: 23842.
- Langenbeck 1776-12-08 to 1851-01-24: 27074.
- Bergmann 1785-09-29 to 1845-02-28: 21701.
- Mühlenbruch 1785-10-03 to 1843-07-17: 21105.
- Gieseler 1792-03-03 to 1854-07-08: 22771.
- K. O. Müller 1797-08-28 to 1840-08-01: 15678.

The pencil note beside Marx, '1796 Nov 25 v. Ett[...]', is not a correction to Marx. It records the birth date of Andreas von Ettingshausen, born 25 Nov 1796.

There is no mathematics beyond this day-count arithmetic. It reflects Gauss's well-known habit of computing lifespans in days. Some entries were updated as late as 1854 (Mitscherlich, Gieseler), within a year of his own death.
errors: Bauer: the manuscript gives 25853 days for 1772-08-16 to 1843-06-01, but the correct Gregorian count is 25855. This is a slip of 2 days, assuming the dates as written (which match the standard biographical dates for the jurist Anton Bauer). It is possibly a misread final digit, but the image shows a 3.
All other day counts check exactly, assuming the dates as written.

results.what: Lifespans in days of deceased Göttingen colleagues, computed from Gregorian birth and death dates
results.modern_name: Date difference / day count (equivalent to a Julian Day Number difference)
results.usually_credited_to: Routine calendrical arithmetic (Julian day system: Scaliger 1583, Herschel 1849)

results.what: Table of birth dates and ages at appointment of the Göttingen professoriate, Dec 1837

deep.surprise_reason: This is purely calendrical bookkeeping. Gauss's fondness for computing lifespans in days is documented in the literature. The only points of interest are historical: the date (the month of the Göttinger Sieben affair), the later updates up to 1854, and one 2-day arithmetic slip.

checkable.asserts: Blumenbach lifespan; the blotted last digit should be 1
Bauer lifespan is 25855, not the 25853 written

transcription_corrections: Blumenbach day count: read 32031; the last digit is blotted, and 32031 is the correct value.
Bergmann day count: read 21701, not 20701 (the second digit is blotted; 21701 is correct).
The pencil note by Marx, '1796 Nov 25 v. Ett[...]', is most likely 'v. Etth[ausen]': the birth date of Andreas von Ettingshausen (25 Nov 1796), not a correction for Marx.
The second number after each birth date (e.g. Gauss '30', Blumenbach '24') is the age at appointment in Göttingen, not part of the date.
